narrative:
The model predicts you have a 30% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. While this might sound positive, students who have never failed before and still show risk often lack the resilience or study habits that come from overcoming earlier setbacks. This absence of prior struggle actually pushed the model toward expecting you to fail.

The second strongest influence is your strong desire to pursue higher education. Almost every student who passes shares this ambition, so this factor worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing.

Third, your low amount of free time after school also nudged the outcome toward passing. Most students who succeed have only a moderate or high level of free time, suggesting that your more limited free time may reflect a focused routine that helps academic performance.

To improve, you should focus on building consistent study habits now, even without past failures to learn from. Since you already want to continue studying after school and have limited distractions, use that motivation to create a structured weekly study plan. This can help turn your current 30% risk into a much stronger chance of success. (248 words)
